catalog_quote: An important consequence of this difference in head-modifier ordering for numeral classifier versus modifier classifier contexts concerns stress patterns of Lao words. Non-monosyllabic Lao words and phrases are stress-final, resulting in pre-final elements becoming reduced. Many monomorphemic lexical items, for example, have sesquisyllabic (one-and-a-half-syllable) structure, in which a primary syllable (i.e. with full stress and with expression of the full range of contrasts in vowel length and lexical tone) is preceded by a reduced "half syllable" (with highly restricted phonotactic possibilities, and no contrast in vowel length or tone). For example, the word kabùang4 'ceramic tile' features a pre-syllable ka- (unstressed, without contrastive tone or vowel length) and a primary syllable -bùang4 (stressed, with long complex vowel and contrastive lexical tone). new_statements.rule_in_words: Lao is a lexical-tone language; in any word (or phrase) of more than one syllable, stress falls on the final syllable. Pre-final syllables are reduced: in sesquisyllabic words the initial minor syllable is unstressed, atonal and without length contrast, while the final full syllable carries stress, full vowel-length contrast and lexical tone (e.g. ka-'buang4 'ceramic tile'). The same right-edge prominence holds in polymorphemic words and phrases, so grammatical morphemes in non-final dependent position (modifier classifiers, class terms, deverbal prepositions) surface de-stressed and toneless.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No rule given. Enfield marks both primary and secondary stress in examples (39)-(41) (numeral-classifier vs modifier-classifier phrases) but does not state where secondary stress falls; full (non-reduced) non-final syllables evidently keep tone and some prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: None as exceptions to final stress. Related facts: a classifier is full-toned and stressed (too3) when phrase-final after a numeral but reduced (to0) when a modifier follows; paa3 'fish' reduces to atonal pa0 as a class-term prefix; in Type A reduplication (Enfield 2004 'Adjectives in Lao' sec. 4.2) the first copy is unstressed/atonal and the second fully stressed; deverbal prepositions and inner directionals are de-stressed and atonal (Enfield 2008: 158).
new_statements.domain_note: Stated explicitly for 'words and phrases' — right-edge stress of the phonological word/phrase, illustrated with monomorphemic sesquisyllables (word level) and classifier phrases (phrase level). Impressionistic, by the language's principal grammarian; not an instrumental study. The statement occurs inside a morphosyntax paper, not a dedicated phonology section; Enfield 2007 A Grammar of Lao (not accessible here) is expected to carry the canonical version.
new_statements.identity_note: Enfield's descriptions are of standard (Vientiane-based) Lao, 'Southwestern Tai, Laos/Thailand/Cambodia' — language-level laoo1244; no separate dialect glottocode needed. Isan (nort2741 'Northeastern Thai') is treated by Enfield as a variety but is not the object of the statement.

sources.locator: p.129 (section 3, discussion preceding examples (39)-(41)); PDF page 13 of 27
sources.note: p.129: 'Non-monosyllabic Lao words and phrases are stress-final, resulting in pre-final elements becoming reduced'; sesquisyllables = unstressed atonal pre-syllable + stressed final full syllable; same stress-final pattern holds for polymorphemic words/phrases; classifiers in dependent position de-stressed and atonal; primary and secondary stress marked in examples (39)-(41) but no secondary-stress rule.
